text: “An impertinence? Oh, father, what terrible things you say!” “If you don’t wait for my death, you might as well marry immediately; there is nothing else to wait for.” For some time Catherine made no answer; but finally she said: “I think Morris—little by little—might persuade you.” “I shall never let him speak to me again. I dislike him too much.” Catherine gave a long, low sigh; she tried to stifle it, for she had made up her mind that it was wrong to make a parade of her trouble, and to endeavour to act upon her father by the meretricious aid of emotion. Indeed, she even thought it wrong—in the sense of being inconsiderate—to attempt to act upon his feelings at all; her part was to effect some gentle, gradual change in his intellectual perception of poor Morris’s character. But the means of effecting such a change were at present shrouded in mystery, and she felt miserably helpless and hopeless.
